articles.title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’
articles.summary: Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architecture. ‘You’re going to Samobor? You must try kremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north.
body: It lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, in Zagreb County’s prettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter.

As well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within the Žumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last.

articles.title: A moment that changed me: I felt hugely self conscious about my skin - until I had a revelation
articles.summary: For years, my vitiligo controlled my life, and I was constantly trying to disguise it. But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approach. The microphone felt heavier than I expected.
body: I was three years old when I developed my first patch of vitiligo on the back of my hand, which later spread to my arms, legs, face and other parts of my body. By the time I was six years old, 70% of me was covered. I was too young to understand what was happening.

Despite this, I had a happy childhood because I was unaware then that being different was something that was viewed negatively. I went swimming, wore shorts and T-shirts, and barely gave my skin much thought. My parents taught me it was part of me and that it wasn’t something that had to hold me back. However, what I couldn’t foresee was how others would perceive me later in life.

My teenage years were by far my hardest. I became painfully self-conscious and increasingly aware that I was different. I struggled with swimming lessons because I was worried about wearing a swimsuit, and during the summer I’d wear clothes that kept me covered because I was embarrassed about how I looked. I wore thick foundation on my face to cover the patches around my eyes and mouth, and excessive layers of fake tan on my body. My skin had complete control of my life.
points: For years, my vitiligo controlled my life, and I was constantly trying to disguise it.
But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approach.

articles.title: Squid ink tomato pasta and honey and fig semifreddo: Chris Leach’s Italian recipes for the end of summer
articles.summary: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome.
body: The secret to late-summer/early autumn cooking is to keep things relatively low-effort, not least to assuage those back-to-work/school blues. And that rule applies across the board, whether you’re making a midweek meal, entertaining or serving up a long, slow Sunday lunch. The sauce for this pasta dish, for example, comes together while the pasta is cooking, while the semifreddo pudding makes the most of ripe figs when they are at their absolute best.
The contrast between the black pasta, the red tomatoes and the golden crumbs is really something else, as are the flavours.

First make the pangrattato. Tear the stale bread into rough pieces, then pulse in a food processor to make coarse, uneven breadcrumbs. Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, for a minute or two, until fragrant but not coloured. Add the thyme leaves, cook for a further 30 seconds, then stir in the breadcrumbs and cook, stirring regularly, for eight to 10 minutes, until evenly golden and crisp all over. Season with a pinch of sea salt and a little black pepper, then transfer to a plate to cool completely.
points: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options.
This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome.

articles.title: The girl with a will to live: the love, hope and pain of raising Elsie – my one in 163 million daughter
articles.summary: She was born with an ultra-rare genetic disorder. After my decades working in film PR, I now face the biggest campaign of all: the fight for her life. My daughter Elsie has beautiful curls – blond like a little Botticelli cherub’s, hair that someone dark like me could only ever dream of.
body: Sound is important for Elsie because she has a visual impairment and, while we know she has some peripheral vision, is legally classed as blind. As a result, she uses her tongue to check her environment. When she’s excited it sticks out, tasting the air around her, licking anyone close, sensing space. And when she likes the taste of something she keeps her tongue out until you give her more. This is how we know she likes lollies.

She makes new sounds every day. If she suddenly realises she’s on her own, she’ll soon make her signature “Ah, ah!” sound until she’s got company again. But at 18 months she is behind in her development and we don’t yet know if she will be verbal, so for now we are learning to understand her in the ways she chooses to show us.

Elsie was born with a rare neurological condition – so rare that there are fewer than 100 known cases in the world. It is a mutation in the RARB (retinoic acid receptor beta) gene, which, when working properly, helps control vitamin A signalling, vital for the proper embryonic development of the eyes, brain, lungs and spinal cord. It is de novo (meaning it is not hereditary), and the effects are progressive.

articles.title: New York Fashion Week’s Show-Stopping Season
articles.summary: Unexpected attention was on NYFW, but for the discomfort and discourse, talent — both established and emerging — shone through.
body: Last night, New York Fashion Week (NYFW) came to a close with Thom Browne’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection, which he presented at the cavernous Hudson Yards venue The Shed, this time with a grassy garden set and metamorphosis theme. Browne, who is the chair of the board of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), typically shows just once per year in New York (though usually not in September), and the theatrics always deliver the right caliber of drama and artistry to end the week.

NYFW often gets chided for its predictability. Not so this season. An incident at Sunday’s Cos show — which involved CFDA CEO Steven Kolb physically interfering with Peta protestors — became the story of the week, as the video of the altercation circulated social media. By Monday afternoon, Kolb posted an apology to his Instagram Stories while the CFDA board released a statement saying that he will be on leave pending further review. Considering the future of one of NYFW’s leaders is up in the air, there was somewhat of a vibe shift as fashion week soldiered on in the midst of the media coverage that followed.
points: Unexpected attention was on NYFW, but for the discomfort and discourse, talent — both established and emerging — shone through.

articles.title: This Restaurant Rocks (No, Literally)
articles.summary: A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. “There’s a rock in the sink!” That was the takeaway last winter after the East Coast contingent of the team that writes this newsletter met…
body: How did boulders become the hot new decor trend at New York City restaurants and cafes?

That was until I met a friend for coffee at the location of Rhythm Zero in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, which looks more like a room in an art museum than a coffee shop. There, a large hunk of stone sat in front of a large mirror next to the counter. Yet another imposed itself in the bathroom, positioned between the sink and the toilet, as though natural absorption for dripping hands making the trip to the hand dryer. Two establishments with big decorative rocks: a coincidence, or an affectation?

But then, I found myself in Pizza 4P’s, an ambitiously and intricately designed pizza import from Vietnam for which six literal boulders were transported into the restaurant from a stone wholesaler in New Jersey. Now three spots? There’s something going on there.

articles.title: How Mariska Hargitay Pulled Off Her Fashion-Filled 2026 Emmys Hosting Gig
articles.summary: “Let’s be honest, it’s a little terrifying,” says Harigtay of hosting. “But I’m in a season of my life where I’ve been presented with opportunities that terrified me a bit, so I thought, why not!”
body: Given the fact that Mariska Hargitay has been steering Law & Order: SVU for 27 years (!!) now, it’s safe to say she was the perfect choice to host the 2026 Emmys last night. She is, after all, a TV legend.

There was even more to celebrate: Hargitay was also the first woman to host the Emmys in 15 years. “When I first heard that, I was genuinely surprised,” Hargitay tells Vogue post-event. “Of course I understand the significance of it, and I’m incredibly proud to be that woman. But I also hope the next woman doesn’t have to wait another 15 years. There are so many brilliant, funny, fearless women who could stand on that stage.”

Her opening monologue certainly did not disappoint. “NBC is celebrating its 100th year, and I’ve been on Law & Order for all of them,” was one of many zingers. There were skits with Taylor Swift, and even a musical number with Andrew Rannells. “I love television,” Hargitay says. “I’ve spent so much of my life making it, and I very much understand how many people it takes to tell these stories and make them matter. So the idea of getting to stand in that room, and celebrate this community, felt incredibly special.”

articles.title: With ‘Book of Hours,’ Ellen O’Connell Whittet Finds a New Path to Justice
articles.summary: Ellen O’Connell Whittet speaks to Vogue about how her Catholic upbringing informed her experiences with pregnancy; fictionalizing her own story; and finding new paths to justice outside of the law.
body: At the beginning of the pandemic, author Ellen O’Connell Whittet was preparing to publish her first book and give birth to her first child. By the time her memoir, What You Become in Flight, hit shelves that April, Whittet had told her entire life story—including her challenges with an eating disorder and a ballet career cut short—with no idea what lay ahead.

When Whittet experienced an act of obstetric violence during her already arduous labor, she knew that she would one day write about it. But, she realized, the story would perhaps be better told in a work of fiction. The result is Book of Hours, out today from Dzanc Books, in which Whittet weaves together the violence that she experiences at the hands of her doctor with her protagonist’s visions of canonized saints.
“I am very clearly not the person that I’m writing about,” she says. “But [that] I could give the experience to somebody that feels like justice.”
Vogue: When did you know that you were going to write about your birth experience? When did you feel ready to write about it?
points: Ellen O’Connell Whittet speaks to Vogue about how her Catholic upbringing informed her experiences with pregnancy; fictionalizing her own story; and finding new paths to justice outside of the law.

articles.title: Using This Under-Pillow Speaker Is Way More Comfortable Than Sleeping With Earbuds
articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. If you're one of those people who can't fall asleep without a " Sleep With Me " podcast droning on, or playing one of those Spotify "Sleep Music 528 Hz" playlists, this week's upgrade is for you.
body: The Jabees Peace Duo sleep speaker is one of my favorite solutions to one of my toughest problems: How do you listen to something all night, comfortably, privately, without wearing anything on or in your ears?

The Peace Duo uses my favorite audio trend, bone conduction technology (pillow conduction technology?). Typically, bone conduction devices send sound vibrations directly toward your inner ear, through the bones of your skull, instead of blasting it out through the open air or directly into your ear canals.

This speaker sits under your pillow rather than in or on your body, which is really the whole point of the "private under-pillow listening" claims. The sound stays close to your head and doesn't broadcast across the room the way a phone or bedside speaker would. Paired with a dual-speaker design, it gives you separate left and right listening units, so you get a bit of stereo positioning depending on how you're lying. Plus, it has a reliable 10-hour battery life, so you can run your sleep soundtrack all night without having to think about it.
